title: Cranberry Juice May Fight Tooth Decay — Study
paragraphs: Mostly grown in North America, cranberries are tart fruits that are high in vitamins and minerals.
They're considered a healthy snack — and one study now suggests that cranberry juice may even help protect against tooth decay.
The study, published in Scientific Reports, found that pure cranberry juice could slow the growth of dental plaque, and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.

Dental plaque is the sticky film of bacteria that regularly forms on teeth. Having some plaque is normal, but too much can lead to cavities, infections, gum disease and tooth loss. This is because, when we eat, the bacteria in plaque feed on sugars and produce acids that erode the teeth.
Cranberries are already used to fight some bacterial infections, because they contain chemicals that "unstick" bacteria from cells.
To see if they could also fight off the bacteria in plaque, researchers worked with eight adults and 14 children, who were all given one of three drinks.
One group was given 100% pure, unsweetened cranberry juice. Another group had a drink that was 27% cranberry juice with added sugar. The final group just got water.

On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived at the laboratory having not brushed their teeth after they woke up, so they'd have a night's worth of plaque buildup. Researchers swabbed the teeth on one side of their mouths to get a sample of plaque.
After rinsing their mouths with water, the participants drank three small amounts of their assigned beverage, swishing each sip around their mouth several times.
After 30 minutes, researchers swabbed the other side of the participants' mouths — this time getting samples from the teeth not used in the first collection.

When they compared the sets of samples, the researchers found that plaque exposed to pure cranberry juice grew more slowly than plaque that was just exposed to water. These samples also showed less acid production.
While the 27% cranberry drink had only an extremely small effect, the results still suggest that cranberries may benefit oral health.
